# Overview

We will analyze a Visium HD section of human liver with acute hepatitis C (HCV) at two resolutions: **16 µm bins** and **segmented cells**. We will run the standard Seurat workflow, compare quality between bins and cells, use deconvolution to estimate which cell types are in each bin, find lymphoid aggregates both ways, and compare T cells inside and outside the aggregates.

**The biological question.** In chronic HCV, lymphoid aggregates and *tertiary lymphoid structures* (TLSs, organized structures with a B cell follicle) are common in portal tracts. Does this acute case have them, and what are they made of?

**By the end you should be able to:**

1. Run QC, normalization, clustering and marker finding on Visium HD bins, and map clusters onto the tissue.
2. Explain how 16 µm bins and segmented cells differ in signal and in what they can tell you.
3. Interpret deconvolution results: estimated cell type proportions per bin.
4. Call lymphoid aggregates from bins and from cells, and compare the two.
5. Run differential expression and GSEA, and recognize results caused by contamination from neighboring cells.

| Time (min) | Part                                              |
|:-----------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| 0–5        | Setup                                             |
| 5–20       | Part 1: Seurat basics on 16 µm bins               |
| 20–27      | Part 2: QC, bins vs cells                         |
| 27–33      | Part 3: Deconvolution (precomputed)               |

# Setup (5 min)

```{r load}
# Load the packages we need
library(Seurat)      # single-cell and spatial analysis
library(ggplot2)     # plotting
library(dplyr)       # table manipulation (group_by, summarise, filter, ...)
library(patchwork)   # put plots side by side with |
library(dbscan)      # finds dense groups of points (used to call aggregates)

# Check versions
packageVersion("Seurat")         # Seurat (6.0.0)
packageVersion("SeuratObject")   # SeuratObject (5.4.0)

# Load a color palette
colors <- c("#0166d8", "#ec102f", "#3aa609", "#b775e1", "#f8d147", "#5ce8ef", 
            "#fd6ca0","#476ba5", "#fea27a", "#add465", "#6524ff", "#fe8f06", 
            "#5cfdc4", "#feafda","#00228b", "#fd5925", "#166d2a", "#a90aa1", 
            "#f3c011", "#5ac7dc", "#c1c2f5")

# Read in the two objects: the same tissue region at two resolutions
obj16   <- readRDS("data/liver_16um.rds")   # 16 um bins (raw counts; you will process these)
objCell <- readRDS("data/liver_cells.rds")  # segmented cells (normalized, with cell type labels)

# Store each object's assay name so later code can refer to it
assay16   <- "Spatial.016um"     # assay in the 16 um object
assayCell <- "Spatial.Polygons"  # assay in the cell object

# Tell Seurat which assay to use by default
DefaultAssay(obj16)   <- assay16     # 16 um object
DefaultAssay(objCell) <- assayCell   # cell object

# Print a short description of each object (genes and spots)
obj16      # 16 um bins
objCell    # segmented cells

# How many cells of each type are in the segmented object?
table(objCell$cell_type)
```

Tell R which cell type labels belong to each group. 

```{r labels}
# Every label in objCell$celltype that belongs to each group (edit if needed)
b_types   <- c("B_cells")                       # B cells
t_types   <- c("Alpha_Beta_T_cells")            # T cells
nk_types  <- c("NK_cells")                      # NK cells
dc_types  <- c("Dendritic_cells")               # dendritic cells
hep_types <- c("Hepatocytes")                   # hepatocytes

# A simpler label for each cell: B, T, NK, DC, hepatocyte or other
objCell$lineage <- case_when(objCell$cell_type %in% b_types   ~ "B",           # B cells
                             objCell$cell_type %in% t_types   ~ "T",           # T cells
                             objCell$cell_type %in% nk_types  ~ "NK",          # NK cells
                             objCell$cell_type %in% dc_types  ~ "DC",          # dendritic cells
                             objCell$cell_type %in% hep_types ~ "hepatocyte",  # hepatocytes
                             TRUE                            ~ "other")        # everything else

# How many cells in each group?
table(objCell$lineage)
```

# Part 1: Seurat basics on 16 µm bins (15 min)

The standard single-cell workflow works on bins too: filter, normalize, find variable genes, reduce dimensions, cluster, find markers. The extra step in spatial data is putting the results back on the tissue.

## 1a. QC and filtering

```{r qc16, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4}
# Counts per bin (total transcripts) and genes per bin, as plain vectors
counts16 <- obj16[[paste0("nCount_", assay16)]][, 1]     # transcripts per bin
genes16  <- obj16[[paste0("nFeature_", assay16)]][, 1]   # genes detected per bin

# A quick summary of each
summary(counts16)   # spread of counts per bin
summary(genes16)    # spread of genes per bin

# Minimum counts a bin needs to be kept
min_counts <- 50

# Mark bins below the threshold
obj16$low_quality <- counts16 < min_counts

# Where are they? Counts per bin (left) and the bins that will be removed (right)
SpatialFeaturePlot(obj16, paste0("nCount_", assay16), pt.size.factor = 6) |   # counts on the tissue
  SpatialDimPlot(obj16, group.by = "low_quality", pt.size.factor = 6)         # TRUE = will be removed

# How many bins will be removed?
table(obj16$low_quality)

# Keep only bins that pass
obj16 <- subset(obj16, cells = colnames(obj16)[!obj16$low_quality])
```

**What you should see:** low-count bins sit at tissue edges, in vessel lumens and in tears, where there is little tissue under the bin.

## 1b. Normalize, reduce, cluster

```{r workflow}
# Normalize: divide each bin's counts by its total, multiply by 10,000, log-transform
obj16 <- NormalizeData(obj16)

# Find the 2,000 genes that vary most between bins
obj16 <- FindVariableFeatures(obj16, nfeatures = 2000)

# Scale each variable gene to mean 0, variance 1 (so high-expression genes don't dominate)
obj16 <- ScaleData(obj16)

# Principal component analysis: summarize the 2,000 genes as 20 components
obj16 <- RunPCA(obj16, npcs = 20)

# How many components carry signal? Look for where the curve flattens
ElbowPlot(obj16, ndims = 20)

# Build a nearest-neighbor graph of bins from the first 10 components
obj16 <- FindNeighbors(obj16, dims = 1:10)

# Find clusters of similar bins; higher resolution = more clusters
obj16 <- FindClusters(obj16, resolution = 0.2, cluster.name = "clusters_16")

# A 2-D map of the bins for viewing (UMAP)
obj16 <- RunUMAP(obj16, dims = 1:10)
```

```{r cluster-plots, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 5}
# Clusters on the UMAP (left) and on the tissue (right)
DimPlot(obj16, group.by = "clusters_16", label = TRUE, cols = colors) |                             # UMAP
  SpatialDimPlot(obj16, group.by = "clusters_16", label = TRUE, pt.size.factor = 6, cols = colors)  # tissue
```

**What you should see:** several clusters that form patterns on the tissue: alternating zones, small islands, and a few compact patches. The clustering never used the spot positions.

Backup: `list2env(readRDS("data/backup/after_part1b.rds"), envir = .GlobalEnv)`

## 1c. Marker genes and annotation

```{r find-markers}
# For each cluster, genes higher in that cluster than in all others
cluster_markers <- FindAllMarkers(obj16,
                                  only.pos = TRUE,             # only genes higher in the cluster
                                  logfc.threshold = 0.25,       # at least ~1.2-fold higher
                                  min.pct = 0.1)               # detected in >= 10% of the cluster

# Top 5 markers per cluster, by fold change
cluster_markers %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%                           # one group per cluster
  slice_max(avg_log2FC, n = 5) %>%                # 5 largest fold changes
  select(cluster, gene, avg_log2FC, pct.1, pct.2) # columns to show
```

```{r known-markers, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 5}
# Known liver markers to help name the clusters
known <- c("CYP2E1", "GLUL",           # pericentral hepatocytes (around central veins)
           "HAL", "SDS", "CPS1",       # periportal hepatocytes (around portal tracts)
           "KRT19", "KRT7",            # cholangiocytes (bile ducts, in portal tracts)
           "CLEC4G", "STAB2",          # liver sinusoidal endothelial cells
           "CD5L", "MARCO",            # Kupffer cells (liver macrophages)
           "COL1A1", "DCN",            # fibroblasts / stellate cells
           "CD3E", "NKG7",             # T cells, NK cells
           "CCR7", "LAMP3",            # T cell zone, mature dendritic cells
           "MS4A1")                    # B cells

# Dot size = % of bins expressing the gene; color = average expression
DotPlot(obj16, features = known, group.by = "clusters_16") + RotatedAxis() + scale_color_continuous(type = "viridis")
```

Name the clusters. Edit the names on the right to match what you see (add or remove lines to match your number of clusters).

```{r annotate}
# A name for each cluster number
cluster_names <- c("1" = "periportal hepatocytes",
                   "5" = "fibroblasts + immune",
                   "13" = "pericentral hepatocytes")

# Add the names as a metadata column (clusters without a name become NA)
obj16$cluster_name <- unname(cluster_names[as.character(obj16$clusters_16)])

# Named clusters on the tissue
SpatialDimPlot(obj16, group.by = "cluster_name", pt.size.factor = 6, cols = colors)
```

# Part 2: QC, bins vs cells (7 min)

The same tissue, measured two ways. How much signal does each unit have, and how clean is it?

## 2a. Signal per unit

```{r qc-compare}
# Counts and genes per unit for 16 um bins and for cells, in one table
qc <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(level  = "16 um bins",                                     # bins
             counts = obj16[[paste0("nCount_", assay16)]][, 1],         # transcripts per bin
             genes  = obj16[[paste0("nFeature_", assay16)]][, 1]),      # genes per bin
  data.frame(level  = "cells",                                          # cells
             counts = objCell[[paste0("nCount_", assayCell)]][, 1],     # transcripts per cell
             genes  = objCell[[paste0("nFeature_", assayCell)]][, 1]))  # genes per cell

# One summary row per resolution
qc %>%
  group_by(level) %>%                          # bins, then cells
  summarise(n_units       = n(),               # how many units
            median_counts = median(counts),    # typical transcripts per unit
            median_genes  = median(genes))     # typical genes per unit

# Distribution of counts (log scale; + 1 so zero counts can be drawn)
ggplot(qc, aes(level, counts + 1)) +                     # x = resolution, y = counts
  geom_violin() + scale_y_log10() +                      # violin, log y axis
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Counts per unit (log scale)")      # labels
```

## 2b. Signal per cell type

```{r qc-celltype, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4}
# Counts per cell for each lineage: are some cell types much smaller in signal?
VlnPlot(objCell, paste0("nCount_", assayCell), group.by = "lineage", pt.size = 0, log = TRUE)
```

**What you should see:** hepatocytes (20–30 µm across) have more counts than lymphocytes (about 7 µm). A 16 µm bin holds part of one hepatocyte or several lymphocytes, so bins average over different numbers of cells in different places.

## 2c. Contamination

```{r qc-contamination}
# % of each cell's counts that come from three very abundant hepatocyte genes
objCell$pct_hepatocyte_genes <- PercentageFeatureSet(objCell,
  features = intersect(c("ALB", "APOA1", "HP"), rownames(objCell)))

# Median % per lineage: immune cells should have almost none
objCell@meta.data %>%
  group_by(lineage) %>%                                          # one group per lineage
  summarise(cells = n(),                                         # number of cells
            median_pct_hep_genes = median(pct_hepatocyte_genes)) # typical % hepatocyte transcripts
```

**What you should see:** T, NK, B and dendritic cells carry a few percent hepatocyte transcripts. These come from neighboring hepatocytes, not from the immune cells themselves.

**Questions**

5. How many times more counts does a typical bin have than a typical cell? Why?
6. Which is better for detecting a rare gene in a small cell: a bin or a segmented cell? Which is better for knowing *which cell* expressed it?

# Part 3: Deconvolution (precomputed) (6 min)

A 16 µm bin can contain several cells. **Deconvolution** estimates what fraction of each bin comes from each cell type, using a single-cell RNA-seq reference. Here it was done with **RCTD** (the `spacexr` package). It takes too long to run in class, so the results have been saved for you.

This is how it was run (for reference only; **do not run this chunk**):

```{r rctd-reference, eval = FALSE}
# Package for RCTD
library(spacexr)

# Single-cell reference: a liver scRNA-seq Seurat object with a celltype column
ref <- readRDS("liver_reference.rds")

# Reference inputs: raw counts, cell type of each cell, total counts per cell
ref_counts <- LayerData(ref, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts")             # genes x cells
ref_types  <- factor(setNames(ref$celltype, colnames(ref)))               # cell type per cell
ref_nUMI   <- setNames(ref$nCount_RNA, colnames(ref))                     # counts per cell
reference  <- Reference(ref_counts, ref_types, ref_nUMI)                  # RCTD reference object

# Query inputs: raw counts and x/y positions of the 16 um bins
q_counts <- LayerData(obj16, assay = assay16, layer = "counts")           # genes x bins
q_coords <- GetTissueCoordinates(obj16)[colnames(obj16), c("x", "y")]     # bin positions
query    <- SpatialRNA(q_coords, q_counts, colSums(q_counts))             # RCTD query object

# Run RCTD in "full" mode: each bin can contain any number of cell types
rctd <- create.RCTD(query, reference, max_cores = 8, UMI_min = 50)        # set up (keep bins with >= 50 counts)
rctd <- run.RCTD(rctd, doublet_mode = "full")                             # run

# Proportions: each bin's weights rescaled to sum to 1
weights <- as.data.frame(as.matrix(normalize_weights(rctd@results$weights)))
saveRDS(weights, "data/Spatial.016um_norm_weights_output.rds")            # save for students
```

Load the saved result and add it to your object:

```{r rctd-load}
# One row per bin (row names = barcodes), one column per reference cell type
weights <- readRDS("data/min_data/precomputed/Spatial.016um_norm_weights_output.rds")

# The cell types in the reference
colnames(weights)

# Keep only bins that are in your filtered object, in the same order
weights <- weights[colnames(obj16), ]

# Bins that RCTD skipped have no estimate (NA); treat them as 0
weights[is.na(weights[])] <- 0

# Add each cell type's proportion to the metadata (column names start with "prop_")
obj16 <- AddMetaData(obj16, setNames(weights, paste0("prop_", make.names(colnames(weights)))))

# check that row names between weights and obj17 meta data line up
all(rownames(obj16@meta.data) == rownames(weights)) # TRUE

# Label each bin with the cell type that has the highest proportion
obj16$annotation <- colnames(weights)[max.col(weights)]

# Which reference cell types are in lymphoid aggregates? (your instructor has filled these in)
lymph_cols <- c("Alpha_Beta_T_cells", "B_cells", "NK_cells", "Dendritic_cells", "Plasma_cells")

# Total lymphoid proportion per bin
obj16$prop_lymphoid <- rowSums(obj16@meta.data[, paste0("prop_", lymph_cols), drop = FALSE])

# Map a few proportions on the tissue
SpatialFeaturePlot(obj16, c("prop_lymphoid", paste0("prop_", lymph_cols[1:2])), pt.size.factor = 6)
```

**What you should see:** the lymphoid proportion is near 0 across most of the tissue and high in a few compact patches. Those patches overlap the immune cluster from Part 1.

# Part 4: Calling lymphoid aggregates, bins vs cells (14 min)

We will call aggregates two ways and compare them.

- **From bins:** groups of neighboring bins with a high lymphoid proportion.
- **From cells:** groups of immune cells packed closely together.

Both use **DBSCAN**, which finds groups of points that are close together.

## 4a. Positions and scale

```{r scale}
# x/y positions of the bins, in image pixels, in the same order as the object
xy16 <- GetTissueCoordinates(obj16)[colnames(obj16), c("x", "y")]

# Distance between neighboring bins, in pixels: for 200 random bins, the
# distance to the nearest other bin; the median of those is the bin spacing
set.seed(1)                                                          # repeatable random choice
spacing16 <- median(sapply(sample(nrow(xy16), 200), function(i) {
  d <- sqrt((xy16$x - xy16$x[i])^2 + (xy16$y - xy16$y[i])^2)        # distance to every bin
  min(d[d > 0])                                                      # nearest other bin
}))

# Bins are 16 um apart, so this converts pixels to microns
um_per_px <- 16 / spacing16

# Cell positions (some objects return outlines: average them to one center per cell)
xyCell <- GetTissueCoordinates(objCell)                                                     # positions
rownames(xyCell) <- xyCell$cell                                                             # name rows
all(colnames(objCell) == rownames(xyCell))                                                  # same order as object
xyCell <- xyCell[colnames(objCell), c("x", "y")]                                            # rearrange if necessary
```

## 4b. Aggregates from bins

```{r agg-bins}
# Bins where more than half the signal is lymphoid
lymph_bin <- obj16$prop_lymphoid > 0.5

# Group neighboring lymphoid bins: bins within 1.5 bin spacings are joined (minPts = 1
# means every lymphoid bin can start a group; eps = radius of the neighborhood around each pt)
bin_groups <- dbscan(xy16[lymph_bin, ], eps = 1.5 * spacing16, minPts = 1)$cluster

# Count bins per group and keep groups of at least 20 bins (about 5,000 um^2)
keep <- names(which(table(bin_groups) >= 20))

# Label bins: "B_" + group number for kept groups, NA for everything else
obj16$agg_bin <- NA                                                              # start empty
obj16$agg_bin[lymph_bin] <- ifelse(bin_groups %in% keep, paste0("B_", bin_groups), NA)  # fill in

# How many bins in each aggregate?
table(obj16$agg_bin)

# Show them on the tissue
SpatialDimPlot(obj16, group.by = "agg_bin", pt.size.factor = 6, cols = colors)
```

## 4c. Aggregates from cells

```{r agg-cells}
# Immune cells only: B, T, NK and dendritic cells
is_immune <- objCell$lineage %in% c("B", "T", "NK", "DC")

# Dense groups of immune cells: a cell is in a dense spot if at least 5 immune cells
# (including itself) are within 20 um; dense spots that touch are joined
eps_px     <- 20 / um_per_px                                                 # 20 um in pixels
cell_groups <- dbscan(xyCell[is_immune, ], eps = eps_px, minPts = 5)$cluster # 0 = not in a group

# Keep groups of at least 50 immune cells
keep <- setdiff(names(which(table(cell_groups) >= 50)), "0")                 # "0" is not a group

# Label cells: "C_" + group number for kept groups, NA for everything else
objCell$agg_cell <- NA                                                       # start empty
objCell$agg_cell[is_immune] <- ifelse(cell_groups %in% keep, paste0("C_", cell_groups), NA)  # fill in

# How many cells in each aggregate?
table(objCell$agg_cell)
```

## 4d. Compare the two calls

```{r compare-calls, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
# Bin aggregates as grey squares, cell aggregates as colored dots, on one map
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = xy16[!is.na(obj16$agg_bin), ], aes(x, y),                # bins in aggregates
             colour = "grey60", shape = 15, size = 1) +
  geom_point(data = cbind(xyCell, agg = objCell$agg_cell)[!is.na(objCell$agg_cell), ],  # cells in aggregates
             aes(x, y, colour = agg), size = 0.4, alpha = 0.4) +
  coord_fixed() + scale_y_reverse() + theme_bw() +                                # undistorted, image orientation
  labs(colour = "Cell aggregate", title = "Grey = bin aggregates; color = cell aggregates")

# On tissue
SpatialDimPlot(obj16, group.by = "agg_bin", pt.size.factor = 6, cols = colors) |
  SpatialDimPlot(objCell, group.by = "agg_cell", plot_segmentations = T, cols = colors)

# For each cell aggregate: what % of its cells sit inside a bin aggregate?
agg_bin_xy <- xy16[!is.na(obj16$agg_bin), ]                                  # positions of aggregate bins
in_agg_cells <- !is.na(objCell$agg_cell)                                     # cells in a cell aggregate
in_bin_agg <- apply(as.matrix(xyCell[in_agg_cells, ]), 1, function(p)        # for each such cell
  min(sqrt((agg_bin_xy$x - p[1])^2 + (agg_bin_xy$y - p[2])^2)) <= spacing16) # TRUE if inside a bin aggregate
data.frame(agg = objCell$agg_cell[in_agg_cells], in_bin_agg) %>%
  group_by(agg) %>%                                                          # one row per cell aggregate
  summarise(cells = n(),                                                     # its size
            pct_in_bin_aggregate = round(100 * mean(in_bin_agg), 1))         # overlap with the bin call
```

## 4e. What are the aggregates made of?

Compare what each method says about composition.

```{r composition}
# Bins: average deconvolution proportions inside bin aggregates vs everywhere else
prop_cols <- grep("^prop_", colnames(obj16@meta.data), value = TRUE)          # all proportion columns
prop_cols <- setdiff(prop_cols, "prop_lymphoid")                              # drop the total
round(100 * rbind(inside  = colMeans(obj16@meta.data[!is.na(obj16$agg_bin), prop_cols]),   # inside
                  outside = colMeans(obj16@meta.data[ is.na(obj16$agg_bin), prop_cols])), 1) # outside

# Cells: % of each lineage among the immune cells of each cell aggregate
objCell@meta.data %>%
  filter(!is.na(agg_cell)) %>%                          # cells in a cell aggregate
  group_by(agg_cell) %>%                                # one row per aggregate
  summarise(cells = n(),                                # its size
            pct_T  = round(100 * mean(lineage == "T"), 1),   # % T cells
            pct_B  = round(100 * mean(lineage == "B"), 1),   # % B cells
            pct_NK = round(100 * mean(lineage == "NK"), 1),  # % NK cells
            pct_DC = round(100 * mean(lineage == "DC"), 1))  # % dendritic cells

# Is there a follicle? Cells with any count of follicular dendritic cells (FDC) genes (CR2, FDCSP) 
# or germinal center genes (BCL6, AICDA), inside vs outside the cell aggregates
counts <- LayerData(objCell, assay = assayCell, layer = "counts")              # raw counts
any_count <- function(g) colSums(counts[intersect(g, rownames(counts)), , drop = FALSE]) > 0  # any count
objCell$fdc_pos <- any_count(c("CR2", "FDCSP"))                                # FDC genes
objCell$gc_pos  <- any_count(c("BCL6", "AICDA"))                               # germinal center genes
objCell@meta.data %>%
  mutate(where = ifelse(is.na(agg_cell), "outside", "in aggregate")) %>%       # where each cell is
  group_by(where) %>%                                                          # two rows
  summarise(pct_fdc_pos = round(100 * mean(fdc_pos), 1),                       # % with FDC genes
            pct_gc_pos  = round(100 * mean(gc_pos), 1))                        # % with GC genes
```

**What you should see:** both methods find aggregates in roughly the same places. The cells show they are made mostly of T cells, NK cells and dendritic cells, with few B cells and no clear FDC or germinal center signal: **lymphoid aggregates, not mature TLSs**.

# Part 5: DEG and GSEA (10 min)

Are T cells inside the aggregates different from T cells out in the lobule?

## 5a. Differential expression

```{r deg}
# Keep only T cells
tcells <- subset(objCell, cells = colnames(objCell)[objCell$lineage == "T"])

# Label each T cell as inside or outside an aggregate (cell-based call)
tcells$group <- ifelse(is.na(tcells$agg_cell), "outside", "inside")

# Compare cells by this label
Idents(tcells) <- "group"

# How many T cells in each group?
table(Idents(tcells))

# Inside vs outside, every gene (Wilcoxon test)
de <- FindMarkers(tcells,
                  ident.1 = "inside",            # group 1
                  ident.2 = "outside",           # group 2
                  logfc.threshold = 0,           # keep every gene: GSEA needs the full list
                  min.pct = 0.05)                # genes detected in >= 5% of either group

# Gene names as a column
de$gene <- rownames(de)

# Raw counts of all cells (genes x cells), needed for the flag below
counts <- LayerData(objCell, assay = assayCell, layer = "counts")

# Flag genes typical of hepatocytes: detected in > 50% of hepatocytes and at least
# 3 times as often in hepatocytes as in T cells (likely contamination)
pct_hep <- rowMeans(counts[de$gene, objCell$lineage == "hepatocyte"] > 0)  # % of hepatocytes
pct_t   <- rowMeans(counts[de$gene, objCell$lineage == "T"] > 0)           # % of T cells
de$hepatocyte_gene <- pct_hep > 0.5 & pct_hep > 3 * pct_t                  # TRUE = likely contamination

# Top genes higher inside, and higher outside
de %>% arrange(desc(avg_log2FC)) %>% select(gene, avg_log2FC, pct.1, pct.2, p_val_adj, hepatocyte_gene) %>% head(15)
de %>% arrange(avg_log2FC)       %>% select(gene, avg_log2FC, pct.1, pct.2, p_val_adj, hepatocyte_gene) %>% head(15)

# Volcano plot: each dot is a gene; red = flagged hepatocyte gene
ggplot(de, aes(avg_log2FC, -log10(p_val_adj + 1e-300), colour = hepatocyte_gene)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6) +                                          # one dot per gene
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey50", "red")) +                # grey / red
  labs(x = "log2 fold change (inside vs outside)", y = "-log10 adjusted p-value",
       colour = "Hepatocyte gene")
```

`pct.1` is the % of inside T cells expressing the gene; `pct.2` the % of outside T cells; Positive `avg_log2FC` values mean gene is upregulated in inside T cells compared to outside T cells. 

## 5b. GSEA

GSEA ranks all genes from "most higher inside" to "most higher outside" and asks whether a pathway's genes cluster at one end. Positive NES = higher inside; negative = higher outside. We use the 50 MSigDB Hallmark gene sets.

```{r gsea}
# Packages for GSEA
library(fgsea)     # gene set enrichment analysis
library(msigdbr)   # MSigDB gene sets

# Hallmark gene sets for human (newer msigdbr uses collection =, older uses category =)
hallmark <- tryCatch(msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H"),
                     error = function(e) msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", category = "H"))
pathways <- split(hallmark$gene_symbol, hallmark$gs_name)          # one gene vector per pathway

# Run GSEA on a DE table: genes ranked from higher inside to higher outside
run_gsea <- function(de_table) {
  ranks <- sort(setNames(de_table$avg_log2FC, de_table$gene), decreasing = TRUE)  # ranked genes
  set.seed(1)                                                                     # repeatable permutations
  res <- as.data.frame(fgsea(pathways, ranks, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500))       # run GSEA
  res[order(res$padj),]                       # most significant first
}

# GSEA with all genes, then without the flagged hepatocyte genes
gsea_all   <- run_gsea(de)                          # all genes
gsea_clean <- run_gsea(de[!de$hepatocyte_gene, ])   # contamination removed
head(gsea_all, 10)                                  # top 10, all genes
head(gsea_clean, 10)                                # top 10, cleaned

# Bar plot of significant pathways after cleaning
gsea_clean %>%
  filter(padj < 0.05) %>%                                         # significant only
  mutate(pathway = gsub("HALLMARK_", "", pathway)) %>%            # shorter names
  ggplot(aes(NES, reorder(pathway, NES), fill = NES > 0)) +       # one bar per pathway
  geom_col() +                                                    # bars
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "firebrick"),         # blue = outside, red = inside
                    labels = c("higher outside", "higher inside")) +
  labs(x = "Normalized enrichment score", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

**What you should see:** with all genes, liver metabolism pathways (for example xenobiotic or bile acid metabolism) may appear "higher outside". They come from hepatocyte contamination and weaken or disappear after cleaning.

15. Which pathways disappeared after cleaning? What would you have concluded without cleaning?
16. All these cells come from one tissue section. Why are the p-values too optimistic, and what design would fix that?

17. Which resolution would you use to (a) map lobule zones, (b) count aggregates across 100 biopsies, (c) tell what an aggregate is made of?
18. Mature TLSs with B cell follicles are common in *chronic* HCV. Why might an *acute* infection have T cell and dendritic cell aggregates but no follicles yet?

**Take-home points**

- Bins give more signal per unit; cells tell you which cell the signal came from.
- Deconvolution estimates cell types inside bins, but depends on its reference.
- Different methods can call the "same" structure differently: report your definition and parameters.
- Segmented cells carry transcripts from neighbors, which can create false DE genes and false pathways.
